cemc-cimc-2020-a1.title: Common denominator 1000
cemc-cimc-2020-a1.body:
The numbers are $\frac{250}{1000},\frac{400}{1000},\frac{410}{1000},\frac{40}{1000},\frac{404}{1000}$. Sorting the numerators $40,250,400,404,410$, the middle is $400$, i.e. $\frac4{10}$.

**Answer: $\frac4{10}$**

cemc-cimc-2020-a2.title: Subtract the overlap from each rectangle
cemc-cimc-2020-a2.body:
Each rectangle has area $80$; its shaded part is $80-16=64$. Total: $2\times64=128$.

**Answer: 128**

cemc-cimc-2020-a2.title: Union minus overlap
cemc-cimc-2020-a2.body:
The union has area $80+80-16=144$; the shaded part is the union without the unshaded square: $144-16=128$.

**Answer: 128**

cemc-cimc-2020-a3.title: Triangular numbers
cemc-cimc-2020-a3.body:
We need $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\ge64$, i.e. $n(n+1)\ge128$. $10\cdot11=110$ is too small and $11\cdot12=132$ works.

**Answer: 11**

cemc-cimc-2020-a4.title: Inner nonagon
cemc-cimc-2020-a4.body:
The inner boundary is a regular 9-gon, with interior angles $\frac{180^\circ\cdot7}{9}=140^\circ$. At $B$, two trapezoid angles (each $\angle ABC$) and one $140^\circ$ angle fill $360^\circ$: $2\angle ABC=220^\circ$, so $\angle ABC=110^\circ$.

**Answer: $110^\circ$**

cemc-cimc-2020-a4.title: Outer nonagon
cemc-cimc-2020-a4.body:
The outer boundary is also a regular 9-gon, with angles $140^\circ$, each made of two equal base angles of $70^\circ$. $\angle ABC$ is supplementary to the base angle at $A$ (parallel sides), so $\angle ABC=180^\circ-70^\circ=110^\circ$.

**Answer: $110^\circ$**

cemc-cimc-2020-a5.title: Bounding
cemc-cimc-2020-a5.body:
Both negative is impossible (the sum would be negative), so either both are positive or $x<0<y$.

**Both positive:** each of $\frac1x,\frac1y$ is less than $\frac14$, so $x>4$; and $\frac1x\ge\frac18$ (it is the larger), so $x\le8$. $x=5,6,7,8$ give $y=20,12,\frac{28}3,8$: pairs $(5,20),(6,12),(8,8)$.

**$x<0<y$:** then $\frac1y>\frac14$, so $y\in\{1,2,3\}$, giving $x=-\frac43,-4,-12$: pairs $(-4,2),(-12,3)$.

**Answer: $(-4,2),(-12,3),(5,20),(6,12),(8,8)$**

cemc-cimc-2020-a6.title: Points among the weaker players
cemc-cimc-2020-a6.body:
Each match awards exactly $1$ point, so $\binom{90}{2}=4005$ points in all.

If $n$ players have at least $54$ points, the other $90-n$ players have at most $4005-54n$ points, but they earn at least $\binom{90-n}{2}$ points from their games among themselves. So we need
$$\binom{90-n}{2}\le4005-54n.$$
- $n=74$: $120>9$; $n=73$: $136>63$; $n=72$: $153>117$ — all impossible (and larger $n$ is worse).
- $n=71$: $171\le171$. ✓

**Construction for 71:** all games among the $71$ are ties, each of the $71$ beats each of the other $19$, and games among the $19$ are ties. Each of the $71$ gets $70\cdot\frac12+19=54$.

**Answer: 71**

cemc-cimc-2020-b1a.title: Keep subtracting 7
cemc-cimc-2020-b1a.body:
The common difference is $13-20=-7$. The next terms are $-1-7=-8$ and $-8-7=-15$.

**Answer: $-8,\ -15$**

cemc-cimc-2020-b1b.title: Four equal steps
cemc-cimc-2020-b1b.body:
Going from $2$ to $14$ takes four equal steps, each $\frac{12}{4}=3$. So $a=5$, $b=8$, $c=11$.

**Answer: $a=5$, $b=8$, $c=11$**

cemc-cimc-2020-b1b.title: Averages
cemc-cimc-2020-b1b.body:
$b$ is the average of $2$ and $14$: $b=8$. Then $a$ is the average of $2$ and $8$: $5$; $c$ is the average of $8$ and $14$: $11$.

**Answer: $5, 8, 11$**

cemc-cimc-2020-b1c.title: Where is t?
cemc-cimc-2020-b1c.body:
- $t$ in the middle: $t=\frac{7+15}{2}=11$.
- $t$ at an end next to $15$ (order $7,15,t$ or reversed): $t=15+8=23$.
- $t$ at an end next to $7$ (order $t,7,15$ or reversed): $t=7-8=-1$.

**Answer: $t=-1,\ 11,\ 23$**

cemc-cimc-2020-b1d.title: z − r = 5d
cemc-cimc-2020-b1d.body:
With common difference $d$, $z-r=5d$. Since $20$ comes $k$ steps after $4$ for some $k\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}$, $kd=16$, so $d=16,8,\frac{16}3,4,\frac{16}5$ and $5d=80,40,\frac{80}{3},20,16$.

Largest: $80$ (e.g. $4,20,36,52,68,84$). Smallest: $16$ (e.g. $4,\frac{36}5,\frac{52}5,\frac{68}5,\frac{84}5,20$).

**Answer: largest $80$, smallest $16$**

cemc-cimc-2020-b2ai.title: Volume over rate
cemc-cimc-2020-b2ai.body:
Tank B holds $5\cdot9\cdot8=360$ cm³, so $\frac13$ full is $120$ cm³, reached after $120\div4=30$ s.

**Answer: 30 s**

cemc-cimc-2020-b2ai.title: Fraction of the fill time
cemc-cimc-2020-b2ai.body:
Tank B fills in $360\div4=90$ s, so it is one third full after $30$ s.

**Answer: 30 s**

cemc-cimc-2020-b2aii.title: Volumes
cemc-cimc-2020-b2aii.body:
Tank B is full after $90$ s, when $360$ cm³ has left Tank A ($480$ cm³). Remaining: $120$ cm³ over a $10\times8=80$ cm² base: depth $1.5$ cm.

**Answer: 1.5 cm**

cemc-cimc-2020-b2aii.title: Depth rate
cemc-cimc-2020-b2aii.body:
Tank A's depth drops by $\frac4{80}=0.05$ cm/s. After $90$ s it has dropped $4.5$ cm from $6$ cm, leaving $1.5$ cm.

**Answer: 1.5 cm**

cemc-cimc-2020-b2aiii.title: Total volume is constant
cemc-cimc-2020-b2aiii.body:
The total water is always $480$ cm³. At common depth $d$: $80d+45d=480$, so $d=\frac{480}{125}=3.84$ cm.

**Answer: 3.84 cm**

cemc-cimc-2020-b2aiii.title: Depths as functions of time
cemc-cimc-2020-b2aiii.body:
Depth in A: $6-\frac{4t}{80}=6-\frac{t}{20}$. Depth in B: $\frac{4t}{45}$. Setting equal: $6=t\left(\frac1{20}+\frac4{45}\right)=\frac{25t}{180}$, so $t=43.2$ s and the depth is $\frac{4(43.2)}{45}=3.84$ cm.

**Answer: 3.84 cm**

cemc-cimc-2020-b2b.title: Equal volumes, then similar pyramids
cemc-cimc-2020-b2b.body:
Tank C holds $496$ cm³. After $t$ s: C has $496-2(t-2)$ and D has $t$. Equal when $500=3t$, i.e. volume $\frac{500}{3}$ cm³.

The water in D is a pyramid similar to the tank, with side $2d$ at depth $d$: volume $\frac13(2d)^2d=\frac43d^3$. So $\frac43d^3=\frac{500}3$, $d^3=125$, $d=5$ cm.

**Answer: 5 cm**

cemc-cimc-2020-b2b.title: Scale factor
cemc-cimc-2020-b2b.body:
The full Tank D holds $\frac13\cdot400\cdot10=\frac{4000}{3}$ cm³. At the instant found above the water is $\frac{500/3}{4000/3}=\frac18$ of that, so its linear scale is $\frac12$: depth $\frac12\cdot10=5$ cm.

**Answer: 5 cm**

cemc-cimc-2020-b3a.title: Prime factors
cemc-cimc-2020-b3a.body:
$216=2^3\cdot3^3$. Three 6s supply $2^3 3^3$, so $P=6\cdot6\cdot6\cdot d$ is a multiple of $216$ for any $d$.

**Answer: Yes**

cemc-cimc-2020-b3b.title: Count factors of 5
cemc-cimc-2020-b3b.body:
$2000=2^4\cdot5^3$. The only digit divisible by $5$ is $5$, so three of $a,b,c,d$ must be $5$, and then $P=125d$ with $d$ odd or at most $2^3$ — it cannot contain $2^4$ (indeed $P\le1125<2000$).

**Answer: No**

cemc-cimc-2020-b3d.title: Last two digits 02
cemc-cimc-2020-b3d.body:
$P\equiv2\pmod{100}$, so $P$ is even, not divisible by $4$, and not divisible by $5$. So no digit is $4$, $5$ or $8$, exactly one digit is $2$ or $6$, and the others are from $\{1,3,7,9\}$.

- That digit is $2$: the other three multiply to $\equiv1\pmod{50}$ (product ends in $01$ or $51$).
- That digit is $6$: $6\cdot(bcd)\equiv2\pmod{100}$ forces $bcd$ to end in $17$ or $67$.

Checking all $20$ multisets of three digits from $\{1,3,7,9\}$: only $1\cdot1\cdot1=1$ (with $2$: $P=2$) and $7\cdot9\cdot9=567$ (with $6$: $P=3402$) work.

Arrangements: $2,1,1,1$ in $4$ ways; $6,7,9,9$ in $4\cdot3=12$ ways. Total $16$.

**Answer: 16**
